title: Gaussian process regression for optimizing L-DED processing parameters in AlSi10Mg additive manufacturing
abstract: Abstract This work presents an experimental workflow coupled with statistical tools to optimize L-DED processing parameters to build defect-free AlSi10Mg multilayer parts. Experimental steps included the quantitative evaluation of single beads, single layers, and multilayers to define L-DED processing windows. Regression and desirability functions, together with multi-objective Bayesian optimization, were used to optimize the main L-DED process parameters to meet target single-layer features. The systematic collection of reliable experimental data was critical to the success of the optimization models, and a detailed methodology is provided. The proposed workflow enabled the production of crack- and macroporosity-free multilayer parts with high geometrical accuracy and metallurgical bond integrity, achieving densities from 99.55% to 99.80% and deposition efficiencies between 87 and 97%, significantly exceeding previously reported values. This work provides practical guidelines to evaluate the outcomes of the AM L-DED process and obtain multilayer AlSi10Mg parts free from deleterious defects.
journal: The International Journal of Advanced Manufacturing Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Aluminum (Al) alloys are widely used for manufacturing components for structures ranging from small to large across several industry sectors, including aerospace, automotive, and electrical. Al-based alloys offer a unique combination of low density and high electrical conductivity, along with excellent mechanical and corrosion resistance [ 1 ]. AlSi10Mg has an extensive industrial application field [ 2 ,  3 ]. Many of its components are currently manufactured by casting, followed by heat-treatment and machining steps [ 4 ,  5 ].

Additive manufacturing of AlSi10Mg alloy has been investigated by Laser Powder Bed Fusion (L-PBF) [ 2 ,  4 ,  6 ,  7 – 8 ] and by Laser Directed Energy Deposition (L-DED) to improve the geometrical freedom with minimum post-processing and to allow for on-demand production. However, laser processing of Al-based alloys offer a variety of challenges, which includes (i) high reflectivity and thermal conductivity, decreasing laser energy absorption capability, requiring the use of higher energy density, and/or laser sources with dedicated wavelengths such as the so-called green laser; (ii) low melting temperature and high flowability, generating molten pool instabilities; (iii) excessive oxidation, reducing laser absorption and material bonding, increasing the incidence of inclusions and unmelted particles; (iv) elevated thermal expansion and a wide solidification range, which increase the residual stresses, and can cause solidification shrinkage cracks; and (v) humidity reaction when Al gets into contact with water, it releases hydrogen and heat, generating combustion reactions [ 2 ,  9 ,  10 ].

In comparison to L-PBF, the processability of AlSi10Mg by L-DED is more challenging. As L-DED usually requires higher laser power levels, the evaporation of low-melting-point elements is greater, which leads to porosity formation. To try and minimize the amount of porosity in AlSi10Mg L-DED parts, hybrid systems with in-situ layer-by-layer laser shock peening treatment following the L-DED processing have been proposed [ 11 ]. Protecting the atmosphere against oxygen is also more complicated, given the larger volumes required by L-DED chambers, as well as the lack of enclosure in many market-available systems [ 12 ,  13 ]. The low density of Al-powders can also impact their rheological behavior, causing an unstable powder feed rate, and powder-laser-substrate interaction [ 14 ]. However, L-DED allows the manufacturing of larger components with high deposition rates, which is a requirement of many applications. To combine the advantages of the two technologies, hybrid L-PBF/L-DED additive manufacturing is being studied for the processing of AlSi10Mg alloy [ 15 ].

Efforts have been devoted to optimizing the L-DED processing parameters for AlSi10Mg. However, even though recent studies have successfully demonstrated that AlSi10Mg processed by L-DED can reach similar or superior tensile strength to those obtained by the conventional die casting method [ 16 ], detailed route for processing parameters optimization, especially in the multilayer setup required for AM applications, is often not disclosed. Process parameter optimization typically relies on extensive design of experiments (DoE) campaigns and empirical or semi-empirical trial-and-error approaches, making process development time-consuming and costly. Parameterization is often the first stage of process development when introducing a new material, machine, or component geometry in L-DED. This stage commonly begins with the deposition of single beads or tracks, followed by progressively more complex geometries to identify suitable processing conditions.

Previous studies have investigated single beads and thin walls deposited by L-DED using AlSi10Mg. Wang et al. evaluated the effects of laser power and scanning speed on porosity, reporting a gradual reduction in porosity with increasing values of both parameters. Correlations between processing speed and bead geometry (height and width), as well as surface roughness, were also established, with higher scanning speeds resulting in lower bead height and roughness [ 17 ]. A similar reduction in porosity with increasing travel speed was also observed in thin walls [ 18 ] and in multilayer geometries [ 19 ]. Heilemann et al. deposited single-bead to empirically selected laser power, travel speed, and powder feed rate for the manufacturing of T-joint wall structures targeting minimum dilution, while achieving adequate single bead aspect ratio and substrate metallurgical bond. L-DED parameter optimization was governed by competing effects among dilution, single bead geometry, and bonding strength. Higher powder feed rates reduce dilution but increase aspect ratio, whereas increased laser power improves melting and bonding at the expense of higher dilution. Travel speed affects both dilution and track geometry, leading to complex competing interactions [ 20 ]. Similarly, Zhang et al. and Gao et al. performed an empirical parameterization for the manufacturing of multilayer thin walls, targeting the minimization of defects and found that increasing travel speed eliminated lack of fusion [ 19 ] and reduced porosity [ 18 ]. Bruzzo et al. also optimized parameters for the deposition of think walls, minimizing deformations and the extent of HAZ [ 21 ]. Although these studies have provided valuable insights into the influence of processing parameters on the integrity and performance of L-DED AlSi10Mg, parameter selection remained largely empirical, focusing on specific objectives rather than systematic process optimization aimed at identifying robust processing windows for additive manufacturing.

As an effort to perform parametrization for multilayer blocks, Ruan et al. investigated the L-DED processing of multilayer structures by varying laser power, travel speed, and powder feed rate to establish a suitable processing window. Process parameters were selected empirically based on the combinations that produced the highest densification. Although the study provides a comprehensive microstructure characterization, heat-treatment response, and tensile strength, it does not address intermediate process optimization stages, such as single bead and single layer. Furthermore, no systematic optimization methodology was employed to explore the L-DED process parameters [ 22 ].

One of the most comprehensive parameterization studies on AlSi10Mg processed by L-DED was conducted by Kiani et al., who systematically investigated the deposition of single beads, and the manufacturing of thin walls, and multilayer blocks. L-DED parameter optimization was performed empirically through an extensive trial-and-error experimental campaign involving the characterization of 54 single beads and 36 thin-wall samples, with progressively refined processing windows after each stage. For the multilayer stage, horizontal blocks were built using three laser power levels (500, 600, and 700 W), of which only one parameter combination produced components with sufficient integrity for detailed characterization. A block with high density of 99.3 was obtained. Despite representing a landmark contribution for L-DED parametrization of AlSi10Mg and an important reference for the present study, parameter selection procedure remained largely empirical and with qualitative classification of acceptable/unacceptable processing conditions. Furthermore, important process variables, such as hatch spacing and layer height, were not investigated. Likewise, deposition efficiency, a key indicator of process productivity, was not reported. The use of quantitative metrics or systematic optimization tools that could help to reduce the experimental effort while improving the objectivity, reproducibility, and efficiency of the parameterization process [ 5 ].

To reduce the experimental workload, machine learning has emerged as a promising approach for process optimization and parameter prediction by combining statistical and computational methods to capture complex nonlinear relationships in data [ 23 ]. However, its application to process parameter optimization for AlSi10Mg additive manufacturing remains at an early stage and has focused predominantly on L-PBF technology.

To optimize process parameters for AlSi10Mg manufactured by L-PBF, Mishra et al. (2026) employed the Complex Proportional Assessment (COPRAS), a multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) method, to rank experimentally evaluated combinations of laser power, travel speed, hatch spacing, and scan direction according to the desired surface roughness, hardness, and tensile strength [ 24 ]. COPRAS ranks alternatives by applying weighted linear normalization of multiple criteria [ 25 ]. However, it is limited to the evaluated experimental conditions and cannot explore the continuous design space, whereas regression models can predict the responses of previously untested parameter combinations. Liu et al. applied a gaussian process regression (GPR) surrogate model to identify the optimal laser power and travel speed processing window for producing fully dense AlSi10Mg by laser L-PBF. Experimental validation confirmed its high predictive accuracy and demonstrated its ability to identify an expanded optimal processing window [ 26 ].

Only recently has machine learning-driven process optimization been investigated for L-DED processing of AlSi10Mg. Zhang et al. proposed a two-step optimization framework to minimize porosity and maximum pore area (MPA) in single-beads as a function of laser power, powder feed rate, and energy density. A global regression model was first developed to predict porosity across the parameter range, followed by a second optimization step within the refined parameter region to minimize MPA. Experimental validation confirmed the framework capability to simultaneously reduce porosity and MPA in L-DED AlSi10Mg deposits [ 26 ]. Although promising, the study was limited to single bead porosity optimization and considered only laser power, powder feed rate, and energy density.

The review of previous L-DED parameterization studies on AlSi10Mg, summarized in Table  1 , allowed several research gaps to be identified. Although studies have investigated single beads, thin walls, and multilayer structures, single layer stage is often overlooked, causing important additive manufacturing parameters, such as hatch spacing, to remain unexplored. Likewise, layer height and contour strategies, which are essential to ensure geometric and dimensional accuracy, have rarely been investigated. While several studies have examined the relationship between L-PBF parameters and the surface roughness of AlSi10Mg [ 24 ,  27 ], as well as the influence of roughness on fatigue [ 28 ] and corrosion behavior [ 29 ,  30 – 31 ], studies on the surface roughness of AlSi10Mg processed by L-DED are limited to post-processing approaches, such as surface laser shock peening [ 11 ]. To the best of our knowledge, the relationship between L-DED parameters and surface roughness has not yet been reported. The most significant gap, however, is that none of the reviewed studies presented a complete parameterization workflow detailing the experimental methodology, data acquisition procedures, quantitative analysis, and optimization tools employed to systematically define robust processing parameters. To address these gaps, the present work proposes a systematic framework for optimizing L-DED processing parameters for AlSi10Mg, building upon the methodology reported by Thiesen [ 40 ]. The framework combines a systematic experimental protocol for data acquisition during single-bead, single-layer, and multilayer deposition with Gaussian process regression (GPR) and multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MOBO) for single-layer process optimization. Initially, single-bead experiments are conducted to define suitable spot size and powder feed rate ranges based on bead geometry and defect susceptibility. Then, single-layer experiments were carried out to evaluate the effects of laser power, travel speed, and hatch spacing, followed by GPR- and MOBO-based optimization to identify process parameter combinations that achieve target geometrical characteristics (waviness, dilution, layer height, and deposition efficiency); Finally, in the multilayer deposition stage, the layer height and contour strategies were optimized to maximize density while improving geometrical accuracy. The proposed framework contributes towards improving process reliability, part quality, and the efficiency of L-DED manufacturing of AlSi10Mg components.

The Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization (MOBO) was selected for this investigation over other artificial intelligence (AI) techniques tools, such as deep neural networks, primarily due to their superior efficiency with small, high-dimensional datasets. MOBO utilizes Gaussian Process surrogate models to capture the complex, non-linear relationships between laser power, travel speed, and hatch spacing L-DED parameters using the limited experimental tests. Furthermore, MOBO accounts for the inherent process instabilities associated with the high thermal conductivity and reflectivity of Al-alloys. This approach provides a rigorous quantification of uncertainty and identifies a true Pareto Front, allowing for a mathematically sound evaluation of the physical trade-offs between competing geometrical properties.

Constrained Bayesian optimization formalizes black‑box optimization with uncertain and even separately observed constraints by placing Gaussian Process (GP) priors on both the objective and the constraints, then selecting evaluations via acquisition functions that account for feasibility. A canonical formulation uses constraint‑weighted Expected Improvement (c‑EI) and an entropy‑based criterion to choose which task (objective vs. constraint) to evaluate next, enabling decoupled sampling when costs differ. Applications span Branin Hoo, constrained topic models (entropy cap on per‑topic word distributions), memory‑limited neural networks (error minimization under a parameter‑count budget), and HMC tuning (maximize effective samples by adjusting leapfrog steps, step size, mass, and burn‑in). This line establishes statistically principled, constraint‑aware search but is typically single‑ or few‑objective, domain‑agnostic, and seldom surfaces uncertainty in a form directly usable by manufacturing operators [ 41 ,  42 ].

A complementary strand addresses when to stop BO. SPC (statistical process control)‑inspired approaches monitor the Expected Improvement process with control charts (e.g., EWMA) and variance stabilization (e.g., log‑normalized improvements) to trigger convergence under noise. These works reduce subjectivity and false positives on synthetic benchmarks (e.g., Rosenbrock/Rastrigin), yet they optimize stopping rather than multi‑objective trade‑offs and are rarely embedded in process‑specific, constraint‑rich engineering contexts [ 42 ].

In transfer learning for optimization, Bayesian reviews catalog mechanisms for borrowing strength shared parameters, hierarchical/random‑effects, and shared latent spaces so that target tasks with scarce data can leverage related sources. Network/meta‑analytic formulations formalize cross‑domain evidence pooling and encode structural relationships among tasks. These methods clarify how priors and hierarchy regulate transfer intensity but offer limited guidance on connecting optimization outputs to physical levers in manufacturing [ 43 ]. At the surrogate‑model level, GP regression remains the workhorse due to calibrated means/variances and closed‑form posteriors for acquisition functions; nevertheless, reporting and using predictive uncertainty in operator‑facing decisions is often underemphasized [ 44 ].

Dynamic multi‑objective evolutionary optimization with transfer learning (e.g., TCD‑DMOEA) targets time‑varying Pareto sets. A typical workflow clusters the population (k‑means), predicts centroid shifts across time windows, and uses SVM + TrAdaBoost to initialize high‑quality populations, mitigating negative transfer. On DF/F benchmarks with IGD/MS metrics, these methods improve convergence and coverage versus DNSGA‑II variants, PPS, Tr‑DMOEA, and KF‑DMOEA, but they require strong initial populations, add classifier complexity, and remain largely benchmark‑centric with limited uncertainty reporting or physics interpretability [ 44 ,  45 ].

Finally, uncertainty‑aware modeling emphasizes epistemic robustness. Recent surveys highlight second‑order treatments (evidential/credal) and Bayesian surrogates; in practice, GPs are attractive because they pair predictions with calibrated variance, enabling risk‑aware decision‑making and clearer communication of confidence to practitioners. However, many optimization studies still treat uncertainty as an internal quantity and do not expose confidence intervals over the operating window used by engineers [ 46 ,  47 ].

Taken together, the gap is threefold. First, prior constrained BO and transfer‑learning‑based DMOEAs rarely address a manufacturing‑specific, multi‑objective parameterization that jointly optimizes four conflicting L‑DED objectives dilution, peak height, waviness, and deposition efficiency under explicit, interpretable process constraints (e.g., dilution and height windows). Second, while GPs are pervasive, few works turn their predictive variance into operator‑facing uncertainty maps and confidence‑bounded process windows for risk‑aware parameter selection. Third, benchmark‑driven evolutionary methods provide breadth but limited physical interpretability linking process knobs (Power, Speed, Hatch Spacing) to observed surface/efficiency trade‑offs [ 41 ,  42 ,  44 ,  45 ,  48 ,  49 ].

Our manuscript addresses this gap by (i) training GP surrogates per objective and running multi‑objective Bayesian optimization to produce a Pareto set that explicitly balances dilution, height, waviness, and deposition efficiency under realistic dilution/height windows; (ii) quantifying and visualizing predictive uncertainty via GPR so that operators see 95% confidence bands across the process window; and (iii) rendering practitioner‑oriented Pareto charts (e.g., Efficiency, Waviness; Height) that expose the physics‑consistent couplings we observe in AlSi10Mg, such as the dominant influence of Hatch Spacing on waviness. Conceptually, this advances constrained BO from generic single/few‑objective formulations toward a domain‑grounded, uncertainty‑aware MOBO that directly informs parameter selection in L‑DED [ 41 ,  42 ,  44 ]. In future work, we will incorporate SPC‑style stopping to further reduce experiment counts and explore transfer‑learning initializations when shifting alloys or scan strategies, building on insights from dynamic multi‑objective studies while maintaining process interpretability [ 45 ,  48 ,  49 ].

The novelty of this work lies in presenting a more complete framework for L-DED process optimization of AlSi10Mg, which integrates systematic experimentation across the single-bead, single-layer, and multilayer scales with data-driven optimization based on Gaussian Process Regression. The proposed methodology explores a broad processing space comprising laser spot size, powder feed rate, laser power, travel speed, hatch spacing, layer height, and contour strategies to achieve defect-free builds with high deposition efficiency and geometrical accuracy. Unlike conventional purely empirical optimization strategies, Gaussian process regression (GPR) and multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MOBO) are incorporated at the single-layer stage to identify process parameter combinations that produce target geometrical characteristics, departing from a reduced factorial design, which contributes to substantially reduce the experimental effort required. By replacing empirical trial-and-error with predictive exploration of the continuous process parameter space, this work provides a systematic and transferable methodology for efficient L-DED process development.

paragraphs: This section describes the materials and experimental procedures required to carry out the present study.

sections.heading: L-DED processing setup
paragraphs: A RPM Innovations 535® L-DED system was used to manufacture samples. This machine is equipped with a Harald Dickler HIGHNO® 13–6 powder nozzle and is powered by a 1070 nm wavelength 3000 W fiber laser source from IPG Photonics YLS-3000-CT. An important feature of this system is that it may operate under a controlled atmosphere, with the entire chamber filled with an inert gas. In this case, argon 5.0 was used to purge the chamber, achieving oxygen levels below 30 ppm for all the conducted experiment steps. To minimize feedstock exposure to oxygen and reduce moisture uptake, which can cause adverse rheological effects, the powder was handled under an inert argon atmosphere whenever possible. Care was taken to promptly purge the powder feeders and the L-DED chamber with argon after opening the powder bottles, which were then sealed before manufacturing. The oxygen level during processing was maintained below 30 ppm.

sections.heading: Workflow for precise data collection and L-DED processing parameter optimization
paragraphs: The methodology applied for the DoE was based on Thisen's work [ 40 ], where the geometries go from simple (single beads) to more complex (single layer and multilayer) steps, presented as follows.

sections.heading: Single bead stage
paragraphs: Initially, a single-bead DoE was performed using a range of spot size (Ø), powder feed rate (F), laser power (P), and travel speed (S), as shown in Table  4 . A total of 36 single beads were deposited using the specified parameters. The resulting single beads were visually examined to qualitatively assess defects, and their geometrical features, including height, width, and aspect ratio, were quantitatively evaluated. Every single bead deposited had its height (h) measured using a height caliper gauge, and the width (w) was measured with an optical stereoscope. Aspect ratio (AR = w/h) was then calculated. Based on the single bead features, a tabular map was created where they were classified as either “Good” (no defects and within the geometry acceptance criteria), “Low height” (h < 0.3 mm), “High Convexity” (AR < 2), “Irregular” (lack of continuity throughout the single bead structure), “Detachment” (single bead without metallurgical bond to the substrate), “Unstable Process (instabilities during deposition)”, with “Porosities” or “Cracks”. These tabular maps were used to define regions where the process occurred without major issues. Surface roughness was also assessed using a contact profilometer (TAYLOR HOBSON FORM TALSURF 50®) to establish a correlation with the L-DED parameters. The influence of each parameter on single bead geometry was analyzed using DoE methods and main effect plots. Based on this stage, a narrower and more stable process window was defined, and a powder feed rate was selected to advance to the next stage of single layer deposition. The estimation of laser energy density during the deposition of single beads (W/mm 2 ) was calculated as the ratio between the applied laser power (W) and the circular area of the laser spot (mm 2 ). The table with the full process parameters and measured outcomes for each deposited bead can be found in the result section. paragraphs: In the single layer step, the more stable and narrow processing window values identified during the exploratory single bead phase were utilized. Within this range, Hatch Spacing was introduced as a new variable in the DoE single layer stage. Hatch spacing refers to the distance between parallel single beads. Three levels for  HS  were defined for each spot size  Ø , corresponding to 20, 25, and 30% of the average width of the single beads selected in the previous DoE stage. Variables used in this stage included the spot size and a narrower range of laser power, travel speed, and hatch spacing (HS) parameters, as reported in Table  5 . The impact of each parameter on single layer geometry was analyzed using DoE methods, main effect plots, and regression maps to identify behavioral trends. The resulting data were used to develop both a statistical regression model and a multi-objective Bayesian optimization model (MOBO), which, combined with desirability functions, enabled the identification of optimized L-DED parameters based on the defined acceptance criteria. As a result of this stage, optimized values for spot size, powder feed rate, laser power, travel speed, and hatch spacing were obtained. For the discussion, the powder feed rate per unit area (mg/mm2) was calculated by dividing the powder feed rate (g/min) by the product of the travel speed (mm/min) and the hatch spacing (mm).

sections.heading: L-DED processing parameter selection using regression analysis
paragraphs: The complete polynomial basis contained more terms than could be robustly estimated from the available experimental observations. Therefore, an initial feature-selection stage was performed by ranking candidate terms according to their Pearson correlation coefficient with the response variable. The highest-ranked terms were retained such that the number of regression terms did not exceed the number of experimental observations.

The initial regression model was fitted using the selected polynomial terms. Statistical significance was evaluated through the p-value associated with each regression coefficient. The least significant term (largest p-value) was iteratively removed and the model refitted until all remaining coefficients satisfied a p-value below 0.05, or until the model contained only two terms. The final regression derived from this iterative procedure served as the representative model for illustrating geometric properties behavior.

It is pertinent to say that Regression coefficients with p-values below 0.05 were considered statistically significant. In this context, achieving smaller p-values is desirable as it ensures that all terms within the regression model exert genuine influence on the geometric property under examination.

sections.heading: L-DED optimization using multi-objective bayesian optimization
paragraphs: Besides regression and desirability functions, to address the inherent trade-offs between competing geometric properties in L-DED single layers deposition of AlSi10Mg alloy, a Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization (MOBO) framework using Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) as surrogate models was implemented [ 44 ]. This approach systematically explores the L-DED parameters’ range to identify the Pareto Front, which is a set of optimal solutions where improvement in one objective necessarily degrades another. The Gaussian Process Regression models were configured following a systematic procedure including kernel specification, hyperparameter estimation, regularization, model validation, and surrogate-based multi-objective optimization. The main implementation details are described below.

For each response, we fit an independent anisotropic SE kernel with automatic relevance determination: k(x,x′) = σf^2·exp(− ½ Σj (xj − x′j)^2/ℓj^2). In scikit-learn terms, this is ConstantKernel(1.0) × RBF(length_scale = [1.0,…,1.0]), i.e., one length-scale per input (Power, Speed, Hatch Spacing). For uncertainty-quantification plots we add a homoscedastic noise term via WhiteKernel(noise_level = 1.0). Inputs and outputs are standardized (z-scored) before fitting and predictions are inverse-transformed to the physical units for reporting.

Unless otherwise stated, we use scikit-learn’s default log-bounds on the transformed space: ConstantKernel amplitude σf^2 ∈ [1e − 5, 1e5], each RBF length-scale ℓj ∈ [1e − 5, 1e5], and when present. Because X and Y are standardized, these bounds operate on a dimensionless, well-conditioned scale.

Kernel hyperparameters are obtained by maximising the log marginal likelihood with L‑BFGS‑B. We use multiple random initialisations to avoid poor local optima: n_restarts_optimizer = 5 for the MOBO surrogates and n_restarts_optimizer = 10 for the uncertainty-quantification GPR. The best hyperparameters are selected by the highest achieved marginal likelihood across restarts.

For the uncertainty-quantification GPR we explicitly include WhiteKernel to absorb homoscedastic experimental noise and render credible intervals. For the MOBO surrogates we used a noise-free fit (no explicit WhiteKernel, scikit-learn default alpha = 1e − 10) to preserve a smooth objective landscape for global search over the small, standardized dataset which is a conservative choice. For optimization runs, near noise-free surrogate models were adopted to preserve a smooth objective landscape, whereas for uncertainty visualization a WhiteKernel term was included so that the predictive intervals reflected the observed experimental variability.

Regarding surrogate validation, we standardize X and Y, optimize hyperparameters with multi-start L‑BFGS‑B, and assess: (a) in-sample residual diagnostics and marginal likelihood (model fit vs. complexity) per objective; (b) posterior uncertainty sanity checks (predicted mean ± 1.96·σ) against observed data for the uncertainty-quantification GPR; and (c) external plausibility by overlaying MOBO Pareto predictions on the experimental DoE cloud (efficiency waviness and height waviness) to verify that trade-offs respect observed physics (e.g., HS waviness coupling). To remove any impression of arbitrariness, we will add K‑fold (or LOOCV, given the sample size) RMSE/MAE/Q^2 for each surrogate, plus calibration curves of predictive intervals, in the revision.

The multi-objective optimization problem was formulated to minimize four competing objectives simultaneously over the calibrated GPR surrogate models. We perform surrogate-based multi-objective optimization using Optuna’s default multi-objective sampler (NSGA‑II) on the GPR-predicted objectives. The four objectives are: (1) |dilution − 25| with a linear penalty outside [ 20 ,  35 ] %, (2) |height − 0.8| with a linear penalty outside [0.5, 1.2] mm, (3) waviness (minimize), and (4) − efficiency (maximize efficiency). Practical constraints are enforced as either hard constraints on the surrogate means (20 35% for dilution, 0.5 1.2 mm for height) or, in the implemented solver, via non‑negative violation terms with fixed multipliers (10^3) added to the first two objectives. Both forms are stated precisely in the manuscript for reproducibility. The search is performed with NSGA‑II over the surrogates (Optuna multi‑objective sampler), using a fixed seed and a reported trial budget, and results (non‑dominated sets and plots) are saved deterministically. We run 100 trials per study to discover a non-dominated set. Results are saved and visualized against the DoE cloud.

The resulting Pareto solutions were analyzed to: Verify that automated optimization converged to regions consistent with the manually derived desirability optimization; Quantify trade-off magnitudes (e.g., 35% waviness reduction when decreasing hatch spacing from 1.99 mm to 1.20 mm); Provide industrially relevant decision support by visualizing competing objectives (e.g., efficiency vs. waviness; average peak height vs. waviness); This method demonstrates that MOBO systematically explores the multi-dimensional objective landscape, providing a data-driven framework for parameter selection that is more robust than single-objective or weighted-sum approaches traditionally used in L-DED parameter set optimization [ 26 ].

sections.heading: Methodological comparison with related data‑driven optimization studies
paragraphs: Recent advances in data-driven optimization have led to a diverse range of methodologies combining machine learning with evolutionary algorithms, Bayesian optimization, and hybrid surrogate models. These approaches differ substantially in their search strategies, model complexity, uncertainty handling, and data requirements. The following discussion positions the proposed GPR-MOBO framework within this landscape, highlighting its methodological differences and trade-offs from representative studies.

Cao et al. use cluster‑wise modelling coupled with a genetic algorithm to facilitate the parameter optimization and microstructure tailoring in L-PBF of Ti6Al4V. The design space is partitioned into process regimes, separate predictors are trained per cluster, and a GA explores mechanical‑property optima. This offers regime‑specific accuracy and strong global exploration, but at the cost of additional orchestration (clustering, model selection) and more hyperparameters and data/compute to sustain fidelity across clusters [ 57 ].

Qin et al. pair deep neural networks with particle swarm optimization for energy consumption reduction objectives. The combination of a high‑capacity surrogate and a population‑based heuristic can model complex, multi‑modal landscapes and scale with data, but typically demands careful regularization and tuning to generalize, and it reduces transparency relative to simpler surrogates especially in small‑data regimes common in AM process development [ 58 ].

Mattera et al. (2025) adopt a multi‑model pipeline combining GPR, random forests, and classification with genetic algorithms to reduce energy consumption in pulsed‑GMA AM. Ensembling helps hedge bias/variance and supports mixed response types, while GA provides broad exploration. However, it increases orchestration complexity (model arbitration, thresholds) and does not inherently expose uncertainty in a form directly usable by operators during parameter selection [ 59 ].

Earlier GPR‑based optimization established principled small‑data surrogates with predictive variance. Yuan et al. demonstrate reliable multi‑objective optimization for WEDM by embedding uncertainty into a robust MOO setting [ 60 ], while Zhang et al. leverage GPR under small datasets to drive a multi‑objective framework for aerosol‑jet printing that explicitly uses prediction uncertainty [ 61 ]. These studies highlight the value of calibrated uncertainty for decision‑making, though their objectives and processes differ from our four‑response L‑DED context.

Positioning our contribution against this landscape, we deliberately adopt a conservative, small‑data‑oriented pipeline: Gaussian Process surrogates per objective, a multi‑objective Bayesian search to identify Pareto‑optimal solutions, and explicit, practitioner‑facing constraints and uncertainty visualizations. Concretely, we jointly optimize dilution, peak height, waviness, and deposition efficiency under realistic dilution/height windows, and we provide 95% confidence bands and Pareto trade‑off plots that tie directly to process levers (Power, Speed, Hatch Spacing) and observed physics (e.g., the dominant influence of HS on waviness). Compared with the richer search and ensemble strategies in Cao et al. [ 57 ], Qin et al. [ 58 ], and Mattera et al. [ 59 ], our choices prioritize data‑efficiency, interpretability, and operator actionability over maximal search aggressiveness.

We openly acknowledge that, in methodological terms, our approach is more conservative than the cluster‑wise + GA and DNN + PSO or multi‑model + GA pipelines. This is intentional for our data regime and end‑user needs: it reduces hyperparameter burden, avoids fragile orchestration under limited samples, and surfaces uncertainty in a way that supports risk‑aware selection on the laboratory floor. At the same time, we build on the spirit of GPR‑based optimization in Yuan et al. [ 60 ] and Zhang et al. [ 61 ] by extending uncertainty‑aware, small‑data methods to a four‑objective, constraint‑aware L‑DED problem with operator‑centric visual analytics.

sections.heading: Multilayer stage
paragraphs: In this stage, to determine the condition that yields the highest density with the fewest number of layers feasible, multilayer cubic samples with 10 layers each and 25.4 × 25.4 × 25.4 mm dimensions were built by altering the layer height (LH), such as to obtain overlayer of 0, 5, 10 and 15%, which refers to the intentional partial superposition between successive layers, controlling the degree of remelting to optimize geometrical accuracy and minimize defects. Figure  4  shows an illustrative scheme for applying layer height. For example, if the single layer thickness for a specific set of parameters is 1.0 mm, but the programmed layer height is 0.9 mm, it is considered a 10% overlayer. For low-melting-point alloys, such as Al-based ones, excessive overlayer may cause overheating, leading to porosity and distortion. Besides, the higher the overlay, the greater the number of layers required to reach the height of the final part being manufactured, thus reducing process productivity [ 18 ]. Fig. 4 Scheme illustrating the overlayer and layer height

After manufacturing, the cube cross-sections were subjected to standard metallographic preparation (sanding on #80–1200 mesh and polishing with 0.3 µm diamond solid-solution suspension) and optical microscopy analysis for porosity quantification using Image J software, with an average of approximately 168 images per sample. For the optimized overlayer percentage, an additional set of cubes was built, with and without a contour strategy applied after each layer, to assess its effect on multilayer geometrical accuracy. An Archimedes scale (METTLER TOLEDO ME204/A) was used to measure density. Each sample was measured five times to obtain an average.

sections.heading: Results and discussion
paragraphs: This section presents results and discussions regarding the design of experiments of single beads, single layers, and multilayer geometries that compose the stages of processing parameter optimization for L-DED processing of AlsSi10Mg alloy. In the exploratory single bead DoE stage, a stable processing window was found, and the role of spot size ( Ø ), laser power ( P ), travel speed ( S ), and powder feed rate ( F ) on the geometry and surface finishing was assessed. In the single layer stage, further optimization was carried out within the stable processing window, with hatch spacing (HS) also taken into account. The effect of energy density on the layer height, waviness, dilution, and deposition efficiency was also assessed, and the L-DED processing parameters were optimized by regression and MOBO methods. In the multilayer geometry DoE, the selection of the optimum hatching space (HS) was conducted considering factors such as layer height, deposition efficiency, and densification. The effect of the contour strategy on the geometry was investigated.

sections.heading: Effect of L-DED processing parameters on single beads
paragraphs: Figure  5  shows that single beads deposited with low  P  are the most unstable or are subjected to detachment associated with lack of fusion and poor dilution with the substrate. For the lower  Ø 1.78 mm, the energy density was higher, and a stable processing region can be achieved with  P  as low as 1500 W, whereas for the higher  Ø 2.54 mm,  P  levels of at least 2000 W were required to ensure stable processing. Single beads deposited with higher  F  were more susceptible to excessive convexity issues, in which higher  S  was beneficial by reducing the powder amount per unit length. For  F , the upper right quadrant was optimum. The  S  was not as critical for lower F, and “Good” single beads were seen throughout the range. However, when achieving the window thresholds, high  S  combined with low  F  leads to “Low height” [ 62 ,  63 ].

The effect of the L-DED processing parameters on the single bead height was examined considering the Fig.  6  main effect graph. This plot shows that the height of the single beads was more significantly affected by  S  and  F , rather than by  P , which agrees with the results reported by Bruzzo et al. that also found that the travel speed is the dominant parameter controlling track height [ 21 ]. For different  Ø , similar average height values were achieved. As the  F  increases and  S  decreases, the height elevates in a nearly linear relationship, as expected due to the elevation in the powder amount per unit length, as seen in Fig.  7 a. Linear fit equations shown in Fig.  7 a allow the estimation of the single bead height based on  F  and  S  variation. Combining the  F  and  S , the deposition rate is derived, which presents a nearly linear relationship with the single bead height, as seen in Fig.  7 b. The amount of the available material in the melt pool can be referred to as linear material delivery density (LMDD), calculated as the ratio between the powder feed rate (g/s) and the scan speed (mm/s). Results shown in Fig.  7 b agree with those reported by Kiani et al., that the height of the single bead increases for higher LMDD [ 5 ]. Although a higher single layer is desirable to expedite the manufacturing process productivity, single beads with excessive height may become too convex. Most cases of single beads with excessively high convexity shown in Fig.  5  were seen for low  S  ranges, which was consistent with the trends observed in Fig.  6 . Fig. 6 Main effect plot shows that the single bead average peak height was more significantly affected by  S  and  F  when compared to  P . This geometrical property was proportional to  F  and inversely proportional to  S Fig. 7 Single bead average peak height showing that (a) this property was proportional to  F  and inversely proportional to  S  because of an enhanced deposition rate, and (b) a linear relationship between the mean peak height and powder amount per unit length

To investigate the effect of the L-DED processing parameters on the single bead width, the main effect plot shown in Fig.  8  was considered. Results confirm those reported by Bruzzo et al. which indicate that laser power has the greatest influence on the track width and dilution of AlSi10Mg alloys processed by L-DED [ 21 ]. This indicates that, while the single bead width tends to increase with  P ,  F,  and  Ø , it tends to decrease for higher  S  ranges. Similar to the average peak height behavior, the deposition rate tends to increase with  F  increment, which accounts for a larger width, as shown in Fig.  9 a. Besides,  P  increase, in turn, enables the formation of a larger molten pool that naturally allows the capture of more powder incoming particles, contributing to significantly enhancing the deposition efficiency and, by extension, the single bead width. Figure  9 b reveals that, for the same energy density, a larger  Ø  contributes to enhancing the deposition efficiency. This suggests that  Ø  is contributing to increasing the surface area of the molten pool. Also, as the nozzle used in this study (HD HighNo 13–6) has a powder focus diameter of 1.8 mm [ 64 ], the 2.54 mm spot size is likely more effective in capturing the power. Besides, less concentrated energy may also increase the temperature of the molten pool surroundings, contributing to an increase in the wettability and width of the single beads. In this sense, unlike the single bead height that is mainly affected by  S  and  F , single bead width was mainly determined by the molten pool size, affected by  P  and  Ø , as well as by the deposition rate, impacted by the  F  and deposition [ 65 ,  66 ]. Fig. 8 Main effect plot shows that the single bead width was more significantly affected by the  P  than by the  S  and  F . Width increases with  Ø  and  P  elevation due to a larger molten pool and deposition efficiency provided. Width increases with  F  and  S  reduction, which can be attributed to higher heat-input Fig. 9 With the (a)  P  increment, the molten pool enlarges, single bead width increases, and deposition efficiency elevates. Deposition rate also increases with  F  increment, accounting for a wider single bead; and (b) deposition efficiency increases with the spot size, associated with a larger molten pool, that can capture a higher amount of the incoming particles

Given that the single bead height showed a strong correlation with the linear  F  (Fig.  7 b) and the single bead width with  P  (Fig.  9 a), the relationship between these two parameters and the aspect ratio is shown in Fig.  10 . This indicates that single beads processed with relatively higher  P  and lower linear  F  produce single beads with larger wettability, which is important for overlapping beads without leaving inter-beads voids in the post single layer deposition stage. Similar behavior was observed in terms of dilution in Fig.  11 , in which dilution progressively increases as  F  reduces and  P  increases [ 65 ]. According to Kiani et al., the penetration depth to substrate is expected to decrease with increasing linear material delivery density (LMDD) [ 5 ]. Increasing the powder mass flow reduces dilution because a denser powder stream absorbs a larger fraction of the laser energy, leaving less energy available to melt the substrate [ 20 ]. Fig. 10 Aspect ratio of AlSi10Mg single beads deposited by L-DED with a Ø2.54 mm spot size. Good wettability was observed when the process was performed with relatively higher  P  and linear  F Fig. 11 Dilution of AlSi10Mg single beads deposited by L-DED with a Ø2.54 mm spot size with the substrate increases proportionally with  P  increment and inversely proportional with  F  reduction

In Fig.  12 , it was possible to see that the main parameter affecting the surface roughness of single beads was  P  and that the mean roughness values were not significantly affected by the  Ø . Average roughness values R a  as low as 2 μm were achieved for higher  P , associated with a reduction in the content of unmolten powder particles attached to the single bead surface, as seen in Fig.  13 . The excessive amount of unmolten powder particles on the single bead surfaces could also be an indication of deposition efficiency reduction, as some powder particles may not be effectively incorporated into the molten pool [ 67 ]. Surface roughness of L-DED AlSi10Mg has been scarcely investigated in the literature. The upper range of roughness values obtained in the present work is comparable to the as-built Sa of 11.2 µm reported by Zhou et al. [ 11 ]. Moreover, despite L-DED typically using powder particles approximately twice the size of those employed in L-PBF, the roughness values measured in this study are comparable to those reported for L-PBF AlSi10Mg, with R a  ranging from 2.90 to 11.30 µm [ 68 ] and R a  from 3.2 to 12.5 µm [ 29 ]. Fig. 12 Main effect plot shows that the single bead average roughness R a  was more significantly affected by the  P  concerning the  F  and  S Fig. 13 A decrease in the single bead average roughness R a  was observed with  P  increase, because of the reduction of unmelted particles attached to the single bead surface

Due to the intrinsically low laser energy absorption of AlSi10Mg, higher laser powers were required to produce single beads within the acceptance criteria, as lower laser powers resulted in process instability and bead discontinuities (Fig.  5 ). Despite the higher heat input, increased laser power could contribute to reducing the surface roughness [ 68 ], in agreement with results observed in Fig.  13 . The larger laser spot size (2.54 mm) increased the laser power captured by the nozzle with a 1.8 mm power focus, resulting in higher deposition efficiency for lower energy density (Fig.  9 b), which contributes to improve the geometrical accuracy and reduce distortions [ 69 ]. However, at this spot size, the 4 g/min powder feed rate produced excessively low dilution (Fig.  11 ) and highly convex beads (W/H < 2, Fig.  10 ), which may promote lack of fusion between adjacent beads [ 70 ]. Therefore, only the 2 g/min powder feed rate was retained for the subsequent single-layer DoE. This first-stage DoE successfully refined the processing window, narrowing the laser power and travel speed ranges for the next experimental stage. Still, both spot sizes were kept in the next stage.

sections.heading: Optimization of processing parameters for single layers
Single layer dilution
paragraphs: In Fig.  16 , the main effect plot shows that the dilution rate increased with increased laser power, scanning speed and hatch spacing. Similar results have been reported by Zeng et al. for laser cladding of 316L on carbon steel [ 71 ].  S  and  HS  variation have a stronger impact on the dilution regarding  P.  When  S  changes, it modifies the amount of powder delivered per unit area. When  S  increases, there is a lower powder amount per unit length, and a greater portion of energy delivered by P is directed to the substrate, increasing dilution. The same effect occurs when  HS  increases because the powder amount per unit length decreases. Because of those conditions, the powder amount per unit length has a higher impact on the dilution concerning  P , as exposed in  17  [ 72 ]. Fig. 16 Main effect plot shows that the dilution of AlSi10Mg layer deposited by L-DED was more significantly affected by  S  and  HS Fig. 17 The effect of powder amount per unit length on dilution of AlSi10Mg layer deposited by L-DED is more significant than the effect of  P . As the  F  increases, the feedstock consumes most of the delivered laser beam energy, and a lower amount of energy reaches the substrate. Still, the  P  increase accounts for more energy available to melt the substrate, which increases dilution

sections.heading: Single layer average peak height
paragraphs: Similar to the results observed for dilution, the main plot effect for average peak height (Fig.  18 ) has a more significant influence from  S  and  HS  concerning  P . The  P  increase enlarges the molten pool, which increases the geometrical properties of width and deposition efficiency. However, due to the high AlSi10Mg spreadability, higher  P  tends to generate larger single beads instead of higher. A possible solution to this issue must be to elevate the powder amount per unit length through  F  elevation or  S  reduction. This property can also be enhanced by using lower HS values. The regions of peaks, which have greater height, are approximated by the closest single beads. However, dilution tends to be reduced, owing to the lower heat-input directed to the substrate, as demonstrated by Fig.  19  [ 73 ]. Fig. 18 Main effect plot shows that the average peak height of the AlSi10Mg single layer deposited by L-DED is most significantly affected and inversely proportional to  S  and  HS  increase Fig. 19 The average peak height of the AlSi10Mg layers deposited by L-DED increases with both the powder amount per unit length and the  P , with the first one being more significant. Together,  F  and  P  account for a superior deposition rate, increasing the single layer average peak height

sections.heading: Single layer waviness
paragraphs: The waviness is a geometrical property of single layers that may impact the porosity of multilayers. Higher waviness means longer distances between the layer top and the valleys generated between single beads. The deeper these valleys, the harder it is to fulfill them, which increases the probability of voids caused by lack of fusion. In Fig.  20 , it was possible to observe that  P  and  HS  have a strong impact on that. As soon as  P  increases, the metal flowability is increased, such as the period when that metal is in a liquid state, thus the gaps are fulfilled and the waviness decreases. The higher the  HS,  the deeper the valleys tend to be that must be fulfilled, so the higher the waviness. In this work, it was also possible to observe a clear difference in waviness for different  Ø . Larger  Ø  tends to create spreader single beads with large wettability that consequently tend to generate smoother surfaces. On the other hand, lower  Ø  tends to create narrower and more convex single beads that tend to generate high waviness. That comparison may be observed in Fig.  21 . No single layers with very high peaks or deeper valleys were observed. This is because the AlSi10Mg alloy has amazing flowability and can create, in general, smooth surfaces [ 71 ]. Fig. 20 Main effect plot shows a strong influence of  HS  and some influence of  P  on the waviness of AlSi10Mg single layer deposited by L-DED Fig. 21 Effect of  HS  on the waviness of AlSi10Mg single layers deposited by L-DED with  Ø 1.78 mm and  Ø 2.54 mm spot sizes. The  P  for each experiment was indicated. In general, higher HS translates into higher waviness

sections.heading: Single layer deposition efficiency
paragraphs: Figure  22  shows the influence of spot size and travel speed on the mean deposition efficiency. The trends depicted in Fig.  23  supported this behavior. This property was considerably enhanced throughout the L-DED parameterization range by the greater spot size. This phenomenon can be explained by the larger area of the molten pool and the greater interaction between the laser and powder beams. The combination of these factors enhances the ability to effectively catch and melt a greater amount of powder particles. The travel speed increase, in turn, significantly changed this property only near the upper limits of both spot sizes, indicating instability in these values. Excessive travel speeds reduce the amount of powder per unit length and increase the molten pool turbulence, aspects that hinder both the capture and the effective melting of powder particles. Conversely, hatch spacing variation affected the deposition efficiency only in the largest spot size. For this, higher hatch spacings contributed to the formation of wider layers with a lower incidence of overlap between single beads, which increases the area deposited on the substrate and consequently the deposition efficiency. It is important to highlight that, for dilution (Sect.  3.2.1 ), the lower hatch spacing generated greater dilution, which is a competing property of deposition efficiency, as it decreased the effective area deposited above the [ 74 ,  75 ]. Fig. 22 Main effect plot shows a significant impact of spot size and laser power on deposition efficiency. A significant mean deposition efficiency reduction was observed at the upper travel speed limits. Increasing the hatch spacing improved the deposition efficiency only at the largest spot size Fig. 23 The mean deposition efficiency values were highest in the largest spot size. Nevertheless, in both assessed spot sizes, laser power increase markedly improved this property

The proposed feed rate per unit area parameter, a variation of the linear material delivery density (LMDD) [ 16 ], provides an effective approach for controlling dilution and layer height and could help difficulties of achieving simultaneously low dilution and high clad height in laser cladding [ 53 ]. This parameter, in turn, can be controlled by adjusting F, S and HS, which account for the amount of powder amount per unit length.

Although the reported dilution values of single layers were relatively high in this work (25–55%), feed rates above 3 mg/mm2 (calculated as powder feed rate divided by travel speed and hatch spacing) enabled lower dilution levels, with little effect of powers between in the range of 1500 and 2500 W. Similarly, our results show that higher feed rates increased average peak height, with limited influence from laser power.

Consistent with Shan et al. [ 68 ], who reported the influence of hatch distance on surface roughness in AlSi10Mg LPBF, reduced waviness was achieved by combining larger laser spot sizes and smaller hatch spacing, while laser power had a minor effect  20 and 21 ). Laser spot size (2.54 mm) was also critical for improving the capture and deposition efficiency, considering that the used nozzle had a powder spot size of 1.8 mm.

sections.heading: L-DED single layer multi-objective bayesian optimization
paragraphs: The output from the Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization (MOBO) represents the Pareto front of the AlSi10Mg single layers deposited by the L-DED process. In multi-objective optimization, there is rarely a perfect answer; instead, the solver identifies a set of optimal trade-offs where it is not possible to improve one property without making another worse. In this work case, five sets of parameters provided represent different "winning" strategies for the single layer deposition.

In Fig.  26 , each subplot shows the progression of Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) predictions across 100 optimization trials for: (a) dilution, (b) average peak height, (c) waviness, and (d) deposition efficiency. Blue Markers Connected by Lines represent the predicted values for each trial, while Red Stars denote Pareto-optimal (non-dominated) solutions. Green Dashed Lines indicate acceptable constraint ranges: dilution (20–35%) and average peak height (0.5–1.2 mm). Blue Dotted Lines express target values: 25% dilution and 0.8 mm average peak height. The optimization converges toward constraint-satisfying regions while maintaining high efficiency (~ 82%) across all Pareto solutions, demonstrating effective multi-objective trade-off exploration in the P (1500–2500 W), S (381–762 mm/min), and HS (1.17–2.0 mm) parameter range. Fig. 26 Evolution of predicted geometrical and geometric properties during Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization (MOBO) of L-DED parameters for AlSi10Mg

Regarding the physical justification of the trade-offs, the output demonstrates clear correlations between L-DED process parameters and geometric quality. Analysis of waviness vs. hatch spacing (HS) confirms that HS is a primary driver; lower HS values generally correlate with improved surface finishes. For instance, Solution 3 achieves a low waviness of 6.41% with an HS of 1.46 mm, whereas Solution 4, with a similar HS but lower laser power, sees waviness climb to 15.71%. The L-DED processing challenges of Al-based alloys are reflected in the dilution stability. Most optimal trials show relatively high dilution levels, with many exceeding 38% (e.g., Solutions 4–9). This is indicative of the high laser power (P) levels required to overcome the thermal conductivity and reflectivity of the Al surface, which inherently elevates substrate melting. Notably, deposition efficiency remained constant at 82.08% across all ten solutions. This suggests that the MOBO model converged on a specific powder-to-energy balance that maximizes material utilization, or that deposition efficiency was treated as a boundary condition rather than a fluctuating response.

Table  10  presents the results of the first 10 optimized trials. Based on the imposed constraints for dilution (20.0–35.0%) and layer height (0.5–1.2 mm), only three solutions (Solutions 1, 2, and 3) fully satisfy both criteria simultaneously. It should be noted that spot size was not included as an input parameter in this MOBO analysis; it was held constant throughout the trials. While the MOBO model suggests a shift toward specific laser power and travel speed regimes compared to previous regression models, the parameters remain physically consistent, and future studies should focus on the experimental verification of these specific multi-objective optimizations through deposition trials. Deposition Efficiency remains constant (82.08%) across all trials because the model reached a "saturation point" where the powder feed rate and melt pool dynamics were balanced for all optimized power-speed combinations. This visualization enables data-driven parameter selection based on application-specific requirements: high-precision components prioritize low-waviness solutions (Bottom Stars), while high-throughput manufacturing may tolerate higher waviness for maintained efficiency. To quantify surrogate reliability before optimization, we computed leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) metrics for each response dilution, average peak height, waviness, and deposition efficiency and report RMSE, MAE, R2, and Q2 (the cross-validated R2) in physical units, see Table  11 . For every left-out sample (N total), scalers for inputs and outputs and the Gaussian Process surrogate were refit on the training split only; the held-out prediction was then inverse-transformed to physical units and stored. Aggregating these strictly out-of-fold predictions yields RMSE, MAE, and R2 per response, with Q2 equal to the LOOCV R2. We tabulate N alongside these metrics for each response and emphasize that all values are computed without any train/test leakage, using the same preprocessing and model specification described in Methods.

sections.heading: Comparison between regression-based and multi-objective Bayesian optimization
paragraphs: A comparison between the experimental data and the simulated results generated by MOBO and regression-based optimization is presented in Figs.  28  and  29 . Since some response variables, particularly waviness and deposition efficiency, exhibited nonlinear behavior and markedly different trends depending on the laser spot size (Fig.  9 , Figs.  21  and  23 ), the experimental dataset used for the regression-based optimization was separated according to spot size. In contrast, because the multi-objective Bayesian optimization model does not have this mathematical limitation, the optimization could be performed using the complete experimental dataset. Fig. 28 Comparison between L-DED processing parameters predicted by regression-based optimization (ø1.78 and ø2.54 mm spot sizes) and multi-objective Bayesian optimization Fig. 29 Comparison between geometrical parameters predicted by regression-based and multi-objective Bayesian optimization

It can be observed that both methods predicted single-layer geometrical parameters within a narrower range than that covered by the experimental data. However, MOBO returned a broader set of solutions spanning a wider design space, which provides greater flexibility for selecting processing parameters according to the desired single-layer characteristics. The solutions obtained by regression-based optimization generally followed the same trends and fell within the range predicted by MOBO.

Both optimization approaches were effective in identifying parameter sets associated with higher average peak height (Fig.  28 a), lower dilution (Fig.  28 b), reduced waviness (Fig.  28 c), and higher deposition efficiency (Fig.  28 d). Nevertheless, these trends were more pronounced in the results obtained through regression-based optimization. Instead of determining a single optimal parameter combination, the proposed MOBO framework identifies a broader L-DED processing window. The methodology also enables the design of AlSi10Mg L-DED cladding layers or additively manufactured components with tailored single-layer characteristics, including waviness, dilution, layer height, and deposition efficiency.

The MOBO optimization methodology was validated by (i) applying NSGA-II to the four GP predictive objectives within the defined process domain; (ii) filtering solutions according to the predefined dilution and height constraints; (iii) evaluating robustness through the feasible-solution rate and the stability of the feasible Pareto hypervolume across multiple random seeds under a fixed trial budget; and (iv) comparing the predicted MOBO Pareto solutions with the experimental DoE space through efficiency–waviness and height–waviness maps.

sections.heading: Experimental validation of optimized processing parameters
paragraphs: To validate the optimization results, the regression-based solution for the Ø 2.54 mm spot size was selected because it predicted the highest deposition efficiency (Fig.  29 d), the lowest dilution (Fig.  29 b), and one of the highest average peak heights (Fig.  29 a), despite not yielding the lowest waviness (Fig.  29 c). This parameter combination is expected to promote higher manufacturing productivity by maximizing material utilization while minimizing dilution and reducing the likelihood of excessive remelting and layer collapse during deposition.

The macroscopic and microscopic features of the single layers deposited for experimental validation, produced in triplicate, are presented in Fig.  30 . The predicted and experimentally validated L-DED processing parameters and corresponding single-layer geometrical characteristics are summarized in Table  12 . The results showed excellent agreement between the predicted and experimentally measured values of dilution, average peak height, and waviness. Although deposition efficiency was predicted with lower accuracy, the predicted value was conservative (86.3%), slightly underpredicting the experimental result, which reached a superior value (92.45%). sections.heading: Layer height effect on multilayer geometries
paragraphs: For this study, multilayer cubes manufactured with the L-DED parameters optimized by regression analysis were deposited with varying the overlayer: 0%, 5%, 10%, and 15%  OL . Figure  31  shows that optimum conditions were achieved for 5%  OL,  which resulted in the best relative density (considering the Archimedes value in g/cm 3 , and OM porosity quantification through percentage) of approximately 99.8% and minimum reduction in capture efficiency and layer height. Further increase in layer height had no positive effect, and led to a continuous decrease in multilayer height, density, and capture efficiency. The productivity reduction identified at higher OL values could be expected because of the Z-axis defocusing from the ideal working zone. When  OL  increases from 0 to 15%, the capture efficiency drops from 97 to 87%. A similarly linear correlation between these parameters have also been observed previously [ 67 ,  77 ]. Fig. 31 Overlayer impact on relative density and capture efficiency. The gray, red, and blue lines and the corresponding axis represent layer height, relative density, and capture efficiency, respectively

Another side-effect that may be generated by  OL  is the multilayer geometry distortion. This effect is caused by the excessive heat-input. As soon as  OL  increases, more energy goes to the substrate/previous layer, and a lower portion of this energy is directed to melt the powder that is being added. This results in more curved side walls, with the highest overlayer sample having a somewhat “smashed” aspect, and an empty region, that is, without material, in the regions closer to the upper layer sides of the samples, indicating excessive preform rounding. In Fig.  32 , the solid white square shows the designed part, while the dashed white square represents the geometry expected after manufacturing, considering the offset generated by the single bead width. Results show that the build manufactured with a 0% OL (Fig.  32 a) did not fill in the CAD expected dimensions (unfilled top right and left corners), but those processed with a 5% OL (Fig.  32 b) or higher fulfilled this requirement. More significant differences can be seen comparing the build manufactured with 0% (Fig.  32 a) and 15% (Fig.  32 d)  OL , in which the latter develops a larger side deformation. It was determined not to test greater overlayer values due to the lack of a discernible density increase, the negative impacts of decreasing layer height and powder capture efficiency, as well as the lateral deformation caused by the high heat-input. Fig. 32 Overlayer impact on the multilayer part geometry. The solid white square shows the designed multilayer part, meanwhile the dashed white square represents the geometry expected after L-DED manufacturing, considering the offset generated by the bead width

The effect of the contour strategy on the geometrical accuracy and surface quality of AlSi10Mg multilayer cubes is illustrated in Fig.  33 . While the non-contour strategy resulted in flatter surfaces Fig.  33  a and b), the use of a contour improved surface finish, providing greater homogeneity and lower roughness (R a ), at the expense of geometric distortions, including edge bulging and lateral material flow. Nevertheless, the contour strategy led to higher geometrical accuracy concerning the 3D CAD model, with reduced dimensional offset compared to the expected geometry, in agreement with previous [ 77 ,  78 ]. Fig. 33 Multilayer cube strategy effect on ( a ) cross-section and ( b ) side view of the L-DED multilayer samples processed with no contour and with contour

This study presents a transferable workflow for the manufacturing of sound AlSi10Mg components with high geometrical and metallurgical integrity. It provides a comprehensive analysis of the main L-DED process parameters, establishing clear correlations between processing conditions and key deposit characteristics, including geometry, roughness, and deposition efficiency. These insights not only support the optimization of additive manufacturing processes but also offer valuable guidance for related applications such as welding and coatings involving this alloy.

Preliminary microstructure characterization by SEM indicated the presence of only rounded microporosity (< 50 µm). Vickers hardness showed a significant increase after T6 heat treatment, rising from 48 ± 3 HV in the as-built condition to 86 ± 8 HV, like other values reported for AlSi10Mg L-DED multilayer samples [ 11 ,  15 ], as shown in the online resources.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: This study presents a comprehensive framework for optimizing L-DED process parameters through a structured experimental approach involving single beads, single layers, and multilayer stages, supported by Gaussian Process Regression models. A detailed methodology for reliable data collection is also provided.

Clear correlations between key L-DED processing parameters and geometrical features, surface quality, and deposition efficiency were established. In single bead stage, height was primarily governed by powder amount per unit length, while higher laser power increased width, improved wettability, and reduced surface roughness. In single layer stage, powder amount per unit length showed a strong influence on average peak height and dilution, while waviness was minimized through the combination of higher laser power, larger spot sizes, and reduced hatch spacing. Deposition efficiency was maximized under conditions of higher energy density and larger spot sizes.

The proposed framework enabled the L-DED additive manufacturing of AlSi10Mg multilayer components free from deleterious defects, relative density up to ~ 99.85%, and deposition efficiency reaching ~ 95%, achieving near-net-shape multilayer geometries reaching up to 86 ± 8 HV after T6 heat-treatment.

Our findings demonstrate that data-driven, surrogate-assisted multi-objective optimization can identify feasible trade-offs within the explored process window; however, several limitations temper these results. Methodologically, we rely on conventional components (independent ARD-RBF Gaussian Processes with L-BFGS-B hyperparameter learning, NSGA-II search and linear penalty enforcement) selected for transparency and reproducibility rather than novelty.

Predictive validation is constrained by the dataset size. While we report strictly out-of-fold LOOCV RMSE, MAE, R 2 , Q 2 , and predictive-interval coverage, these metrics quantify interpolation within the sampled domain and do not guarantee extrapolation or robustness to process drift. The desirability targets and constraint windows reflect informed but manually selected criteria; alternative weightings, penalty multipliers, or acceptance thresholds could shift the recommended settings. Likewise, MOBO outcomes depend on surrogate fidelity and the selected random seeds and trial budgets. These effects were mitigated through fixed seeds and sensitivity analyses; however, global optimality is not claimed.

Practical trade-offs also include the higher computational cost of MOBO compared with regression-based desirability optimization and differences in model interpretability, with explicit regression coefficients versus permutation and partial-dependence analyses for the Gaussian Process surrogates. Furthermore, transferability remains an open challenge, as kernels, hyperparameters, and constraint windows would require re-estimation for different alloys, machines, scan strategies, or geometries. In addition, unmodeled physical phenomena, such as melt-pool hydrodynamics and oxidation, may limit the portability of the proposed framework.

Future work will focus on prospective experimental validation of the recommended parameter sets, feasibility-aware optimization incorporating uncertainty and safety constraints, automated elicitation of multi-objective preferences to replace manually defined desirability criteria, physics-informed or hybrid surrogate models, and cross-platform studies to assess the generalizability of the proposed framework beyond the present alloy, machine, and geometry combination.
